name: Prostamax
lead: Prostamax is a synthetic tetrapeptide with the sequence Lys-Glu-Asp-Pro (KEDP), developed by Russian gerontologist Vladimir Khavinson and colleagues at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology as one of a series of short-peptide "bioregulators" [1]. It was designed around the amino acid composition of Prostatilen, a prostate-tissue extract preparation, and is described by its developers as acting on prostate tissue [1].

In looksmaxxing and longevity circles it appears as a niche "research peptide" in the same family as Epithalon, and its link to appearance is through the claimed anti-aging and tissue-support effects of the Khavinson peptide family rather than any direct cosmetic action. People who use bioregulator peptides generally aim to slow visible and functional ageing; whether Prostamax does this in people has not been tested.

Published work on Prostamax consists of cell-culture and animal experiments plus in vitro studies of lymphocytes from elderly donors, mostly from the Khavinson group and collaborators, reporting effects on chromatin structure [2][3][4]. No clinical trials were found.

paras: Prostamax is a linear tetrapeptide, H-Lys-Glu-Asp-Pro-OH, with molecular formula C20H33N5O9 and molecular weight around 487.5 g/mol, according to Grokipedia, an AI-generated source that has not been independently verified [1]. It belongs to the Khavinson series of tissue-specific bioregulators, typically composed of two to four amino acids and designed from the amino acid assay of natural organ extracts [1]. Prostamax was constructed on the basis of Prostatilen, an earlier peptide preparation derived from prostate extracts [1].

Grokipedia places the peptide in Khavinson's research programme on short-chain bioregulators during the 1980s and 1990s, at an institute it says was established in 1992, with the aim of making synthetic analogues of natural tissue-derived peptide extracts [1]. It lists Prostamax alongside Epithalon, Livagen, Vilon, Cortagen and other peptides from the same laboratory [1][2].

Khavinson (1946 to 2024) directed the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and headed a gerontology department at North-Western State Medical University, according to Wikipedia.[9] The same page credits him with extracting more than 20 peptide complexes from organs and synthesising 15 others between 1973 and 2013, and states that six peptide medicines were approved for medical use in the USSR, Russia and other CIS countries; it describes these tallies, and the claim that the peptides lack toxic or adverse effects, as resting on his own studies, and it carries a notice about promotional content.[9] Most published Prostamax work comes from this research group and appeared in Russian and Georgian journals.[2][3][6]

Proponents of the Khavinson bioregulator concept propose that short peptides enter cells and nuclei and interact with DNA and chromatin, altering gene expression [1][5]. For Prostamax, in vitro studies on lymphocytes from people aged about 75 to 88 report that the peptide caused decondensation of heterochromatin and activation of ribosomal genes [2][3][6]. These findings come from cultured cells, and their relevance to prostate function or appearance has not been tested in people.

In organ-culture experiments, a very low concentration (0.05 ng/ml) of Prostamax and other synthetic peptides stimulated explants of prostate, heart, lung and pancreas tissue from 3-week-old and 18-month-old rats, according to the authors, who suggested the peptides could be used to stimulate reparative processes in ageing tissues [4].

A study of lymphocytes from donors aged 75 to 86 reported that Prostamax raised the frequency of sister chromatid exchanges from 5.9 to 12.0 per cell, raised Ag-positive nucleolar organiser regions from 0.95 to 2.5 per cell and reduced large pericentromeric heterochromatin variants on chromosomes 1 and 9 [3]. A microcalorimetry study found that Prostamax shifted chromatin denaturation endotherms to lower temperatures by 2.9 and 1.0 degrees C, which the authors connected to partial relaxation of chromatin fibres [6]. A separate study examined how Prostamax and copper or cadmium ions affected the thermal stability of chromatin in cultured lymphocytes from older people [7]. A laboratory study found that several short peptides, including related Khavinson peptides, can enter HeLa cells and nuclei [5].
No studies found. Related work is limited to cell-culture and animal-tissue experiments, described above.

Prostamax is not approved as a medicine by major regulators and is sold in gray-market channels as a research chemical, according to the Grokipedia summary [1]. Little looksmaxxing-specific discussion could be sourced. The name is also used for an over-the-counter herbal prostate supplement: a 2017 T Nation poster says he ordered a product called Prostamax, a 'natural alternative' containing dwarf palmetto berries and pumpkin seeds, after a bad experience with the antibiotic doxycycline for prostatitis [8]. That product is distinct from the Khavinson peptide.

card.summary: A four-amino-acid Russian "bioregulator" peptide tied to prostate support; only cell and rat-tissue work exists.
card.note: No human trials; unregulated research-chemical product.

quick.overview:
Prostamax is a four-amino-acid peptide (Lys-Glu-Asp-Pro) from the Khavinson group in St. Petersburg, part of a family of short bioregulator peptides marketed for aging and organ-specific support. Its supposed target is the prostate.

Published work is limited to cultured cells and rat tissue, mostly from the developers' circle. No human trials were found, and its link to appearance is indirect.
quick.mechanism: Proponents propose that the peptide enters cell nuclei and loosens condensed chromatin, changing gene expression. This has been reported in lymphocytes from elderly donors in vitro.
quick.risks: No human safety data from trials were found. It has no regulatory approval for human use and is sold as a research chemical, so product purity is not assured.

chain: Short peptide proposed to enter cells and interact with chromatin
Heterochromatin decondensation and gene activation reported in cultured aged cells
Claimed tissue-specific normalisation and anti-aging effect
Appearance benefit is a claimed downstream effect
angle.text: Prostamax is discussed as a bioregulator that supports prostate tissue and, as part of the Khavinson peptide family, healthy ageing. The appearance connection is the claimed anti-aging effect; the evidence is limited to cell and rat-tissue studies.
